items.take: Your code can be perfect and you can still get robbed — because the thief didn't break your lock, they stole the key from the locksmith. The pattern: the attack surface is never just your smart contract. It's everything around it — the host, the dashboard, the env vars. If you keep private keys or API secrets in ANY cloud dashboard, rotate them today, not after the announcement. Secrets are like toothbrushes: replace them regularly, never share them.
items.title: Railway breach leaks customer secrets — ~$371K in crypto drained across 19 chains
items.what: Cloud host Railway disclosed that an unauthorized party may have accessed customer environment variables — the secret settings where projects keep API keys, database passwords, and even private keys. Blockchain researcher Taylor Monahan traced roughly $371,000 in crypto theft across 19 EVM chains to the breach: 500+ transactions from 200+ addresses, drained with a standard wallet-sweeper script. The first theft transaction landed at 19:36 UTC on Oct 21 — hours before Railway's public announcement. Railway paused builds and told customers to rotate credentials. Railway has not independently confirmed the $371K figure.

items.take: An exchange says 'funds are safe.' The chain's best detective says your old hacked wallets are still shaking hands with your hot wallets. Who do you believe — the press release or the blockchain? The blockchain doesn't do PR. The pattern: after a hack, 'we fixed it' means nothing until the compromised addresses are dead and buried. Don't listen to what they SAY. Watch what the wallets DO.
items.title: CoinDCX denies new $16M hack as ZachXBT challenges their story
items.what: India's largest exchange CoinDCX denied claims of a fresh breach after ~$16M in USDT and 5,783 TRX moved from wallets linked to the exchange. CoinDCX says the addresses were compromised in their July 2025 hack and are no longer part of active infrastructure — 'users' funds are safe.' Blockchain investigator ZachXBT disputed that, showing at least one of the addresses kept handling deposits and touching CoinDCX's current hot wallets months after the supposed cleanup. No new customer losses are independently confirmed.

items.take: This is the good news nobody shares — and we share the good too. Sometimes the system works: a clear bounty, no games, the hacker walks away rich and legal, users get their money back. The pattern worth copying: every protocol should publish its bounty number BEFORE the hack, not negotiate it after. A $5M bounty is expensive. Losing $42M is worse.
items.title: $42M GMX hacker goes white-hat — returns everything for a $5M bounty
items.what: The hacker behind the $42M GMX exploit (a re-entrancy attack on GMX V1) has returned the funds in exchange for a $5,000,000 bounty, going white-hat. GMX confirmed the exploit was contained to V1 — V2 markets, liquidity pools, and the ecosystem were unaffected. GMX's token jumped ~18% on the news.

items.take: The hardware wallet was never broken. Their TRUST was. A push notification, a fake site, a countdown timer to create panic — $2.56M in six hours. The pattern: urgency is the weapon. Any message that makes you act FAST is trying to make you think SLOW. Tattoo this on your brain: no real security alert will ever ask for your recovery phrase. Not ever. Not once.
items.title: Fake 'security alerts' drain $2.56M from hardware wallet users in 6 hours
items.what: Attackers compromised a third-party notification service used by NGRAVE's LIQUID phone app (companion to its ZERO hardware wallet) and pushed fake security alerts on Oct 17 claiming users' portfolios had synced with a new device. Victims who tapped through landed on a cloned NGRAVE site with a countdown timer; 'denying' the sync led to a page harvesting recovery phrases. ~$2.56M was stolen across 70 wallets on four networks in about six hours — mostly BTC and ETH, later routed toward Monero. NGRAVE disabled notifications during the investigation.

items.take: The company that sells 'we lock your tokens so nobody can steal them' just got its locks picked. The irony writes itself — but the lesson is serious: 'audited' is a moment in time, not a permanent state. Even the lock-makers get robbed. The pattern: shared pools are shared risk. When many projects' locked tokens sit in one contract, one clever bug becomes everybody's problem. Ask where your locked tokens actually sit — and who else is in the pool with you.
items.title: The token-LOCKING platform gets drained: $86K exploit hits UNCX vesting pool
items.what: UNCX Network (formerly UniCrypt) — whose entire business is locking tokens so insiders can't sell early — lost ~$86,000 from its shared vesting pool on Ethereum. Per security firm Blockaid, the attacker opened several vesting positions, released one large position, topped up the pool, then cancelled a position in a way that left a tiny leftover slot able to withdraw OTHER users' tokens. Ten tokens across four chains were affected. UNCX paused new positions, raised fees, and says its liquidity lockers are unaffected. Funds remain missing.
